a2-le-completed.title: Completed Actions (le)
a2-le-completed.explanation: The particle le placed right after a verb marks that the action is completed or has happened -- roughly like English's past tense, though le itself marks completion/change, not time. To negate a completed action, don't use bù + le together -- use hái méi (yǒu) + verb ('haven't ... yet') instead, and drop le entirely.
a2-le-completed.fact: le has two very different jobs that beginners often mix up: right after a verb (chī le, 'ate') it marks a completed action; at the very end of a sentence (Wǒ è le, 'I've become hungry') it marks a change of state. The same sentence can even carry both at once.

dialogue.en: Yes I have, thanks. And you?

dialogue.native: Wǒ hái méi chī. Wǒ è le.

a2-future.title: Future Actions (yào vs huì)
a2-future.explanation: Both yào and huì can point to the future, but they answer different questions. yào expresses intention or plan -- 'going to / want to' -- something you've decided to do. huì expresses either a learned ability ('can/know how to') or a prediction about what will happen, closer to English 'will'.
a2-future.fact: huì is also the word for skills you've learned, with no future meaning at all: Wǒ huì shuō Zhōngwén ('I can speak Chinese') is about ability right now, not something that will happen later. Context, not the word itself, tells you which sense of huì is meant.

dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.native: Wǒ yào qù kàn diànyǐng. Nǐ huì lái ma?
dialogue.en: I'm going to see a movie. Will you come?

a2-comparison.title: Comparisons (bǐ)
a2-comparison.explanation: To say A is more [adjective] than B, put bǐ directly between the two things being compared, followed by a plain adjective -- no hěn or other degree word goes in front of it (that's for stating a quality alone, not comparing). To compare a specific amount, add the difference after the adjective: A bǐ B dà liǎng suì ('A is two years older than B').
a2-comparison.fact: For 'not as ... as', don't use bù bǐ -- that actually sounds like a debate over the comparison itself. The natural way is méiyǒu: A méiyǒu B (nàme) adjective, literally 'A doesn't have B's amount of that quality'.

dialogue.native: Zhège shǒujī bǐ nàge guì ma?
dialogue.en: Is this phone more expensive than that one?

dialogue.native: Bǐ nàge guì yìdiǎn, dànshì gèng hǎo yòng.
dialogue.en: It's a bit more expensive than that one, but easier to use.

a2-because-so.title: Because...So (yīnwèi...suǒyǐ)
a2-because-so.explanation: Chinese pairs the two halves of a because-clause explicitly: yīnwèi introduces the reason, suǒyǐ introduces the result -- unlike English, where using both 'because' and 'so' in one sentence feels redundant, in Chinese it's the normal, expected pattern. Either half can also stand alone once the connection is already clear from context.
a2-because-so.fact: The reason-clause doesn't have to come first. Wǒ méi qù, yīnwèi méiyǒu shíjiān ('I didn't go, because I had no time') puts the result before yīnwèi -- but when the result comes second like that, suǒyǐ is dropped, since pairing yīnwèi...suǒyǐ that way would sound like the sentence is repeating itself.

dialogue.native: Yīnwèi wǒ bìng le, suǒyǐ méi lái.
dialogue.en: Because I was sick, so I didn't come.
Are you feeling a bit better now?
